Messages.Author: Alec Habig
Messages.Body:
NCascone <ncas...@aol.com> wrote:
>While I wouldn't call this a "debate", since it's not a contest, I'm
>interested in knowing what the 4CL side needs to "rebut"? Just out of
>curiosity . . .

Umm... thinking... (this was a couple weeks ago, all the posts are long
expired..)

ah! ok, data retrieved from long term memory :)

In the previous debate, the arguments ran as such :

NL:
if you fix vote pushing and repeat actions on untaps, there are no
"degenerate" decks that are unstoppable. The game is self-balancing.

under 4CL, it pays to have a lot of cards, so that you can use 4 of
each similar common plus 4 of each similar rare to make a focused deck.

under 4CL, the number of different +stealth and +bleed cards available means
that a focused Malk S&B is quite possible, while such a deck's natural enemy
(a rush combat deck) cannot be made (along with most other deck styles).

4CL:
for really new players, it's hard to get more than 4 of a needed common
anyway, so a 4CL tries to balance the field between new and experienced
players.

At least, these are the arguments on both sides that I never saw satisfactorily
rebutted. The two arguments against 4CL's remaining point have two weak
counters :

The needed commons can be easily traded for from the experienced players or
bought bulk for a few cents per card;

even under 4CL, the experienced players have the advantage of having 4 of the
similar rares to back up his 4 commons.

I haven't seen a good counter to the NL arguments. The 4CL proponents
invariably fall back on "well, we like it" rather than addressing the points.
Which is fine. It is, after all, a game to be played such that you like it and
have fun, but it is not a satisfactory debate on the topic, as was claimed by
the person I followed up to.

Okay, one last 4cl argument that I haven't really seen addressed: in 4cl
the fifth through fortieth extra cards aren't all that useful, and I've
seen them given away to new players to give them a better starting
chance. I've done this myself, because I think it's in my best
interests to have as many people playing Jyhad as possible; I don't
think I would have too much of an impetus to do this under no limits.
It may have been Curt Adams who wrote that and ideal number of WWEF
can be obtained by opening only *two* booster starter boxes (pardon me
if it isn't). This seems to be a prohibitive entrance fee to get a
sufficient amount of *commons*, of all things...

TJH

OK, let me take a mild stab at it . . .

I'm not sure the "one-vote-per Meth" "fix" on vote pushing works. Suppose
my vote deck gets behind in votes because someone else's Justicar comes
out before I get any voting vamps. If I'm limited to one vote per PA,
doesn't that rather hurt my Political deck? Calling a vote is a 1-stealth

action, easily blocked. All the vote cards in the world won't help you in
the ensuing combat. If NL needs this "fix", it seems pretty unstable . .
. ditto for repeat actions. CL fixes both these problems.

I've never agreed with the concept that more cards are needed under CL.
Most of the "similar effect" cards are commons/uncommons anyway. Other
than Kine Dominance, I can't think of a rare that I regularly include in
my decks at the limit (plus, I only have 3 KD).

I saw at least 1 Brujah Rush deck posted under CL. The leading NL
proponent dismissed it because "real Brujah don't use guns". Hardly a

definitive counterargument . . . I'll try building a Rush deck for my next
game, and then post the results. Still, it seems like there are plenty of
force-a-combat cards to deal with a S&B if you're not the prey. If you
are the prey, you need to use the multi-player dynamic to get the others
to help eliminate the Malk before they start scoring big. This has been
cited as a negative; to me it's a matter of taste.

To sum up, I think the Malk S&B situation is the biggest argument to

playing with CL. I plan to try my hand at building a Rush deck under 4CL.

Messages.Author: Alec Habig
Messages.Body:
NCascone <ncas...@aol.com> wrote:
>I'm not sure the "one-vote-per Meth" "fix" on vote pushing works. Suppose
>my vote deck gets behind in votes because someone else's Justicar comes
>out before I get any voting vamps. If I'm limited to one vote per PA,
>doesn't that rather hurt my Political deck?

No, not really. It just means that you can't use a handful of PA cards for
your votes. You'll have to use those nice presence based plus vote cards, for
instance. Without a limit of one PA per meth, there's simply no reason to ever
use cards like Bewitching Oration. Or, for that matter, any of the other more
convoluted cards that deal with voting/politics. Simply put PA cards in the
deck instead, they're always worth a free vote, and you can always use them
as an action, too!

>Calling a vote is a 1-stealth action, easily blocked. All the vote cards in
>the world won't help you in the ensuing combat.

Quite true, but irrelevant to the question. When getting intercepted, it
doesn't matter if you've got 8 million votes or one.

>If NL needs this "fix", it seems pretty unstable . .

Huh? Even under 4CL, vote pushing is king. Just put four of every PA in your
deck. One's as good as another when it comes to getting more votes to pass
something.

> ditto for repeat actions. CL fixes both these problems.

Yes. Note what I said : "if you add the following two fixes ... degenerate
decks don't really work under NL". I simply feel that 4CL is like fixing a
short circuit by smashing the circuitboard with a mallet. "Look ma, no more
short!!" I'd much rather fix the specific problem (repeat actions) than change
the way the whole game works.

>I've never agreed with the concept that more cards are needed under CL.
>Most of the "similar effect" cards are commons/uncommons anyway. Other
>than Kine Dominance, I can't think of a rare that I regularly include in
>my decks at the limit (plus, I only have 3 KD).

Fists of Death. Flesh of Marble. Psychic Veil. And that's just off the top
of my head. I've never seen a DS card, so I don't know if they've done the
MtG thing of adding more similar cards, but it could be even worse.

BTW, it's looking like a fix for Thoughts Betrayed should join the above two
fixes. However, I've never even seen the card, so can't comment on that :)

Peace be with you,

CL doesn't prevent degenerate wienie vote deck, it just makes them more
expensive. So, you can only include four KRC, four CA, four Sabbat Threat,
four Paradigm Shift. Just throw in any other vote that can do damage,
like Domain Chalenge (sp) or Autarkis Persecusion (I may have that backwards).
Suppliment your deck with plenty of Praxi and you'll be able to pass every
vote that you want. This is terribly boring. One of the local players didn't
like the idea of one vote each, but he quickly adapted by adding Ventrue HQ,
a couple of Justicar votes, and a couple of Princes in his crypt. Being
limited to 1 vote/PA does "limit" purely political decks, but not cripple
them like 4CL does to rush combat. One of the advantages of 4CL is supposed
to be enforced diversity, i.e.: you can only have a few of the cards you
really want so are forced to broaden you deck to make it effective (see all
the posted attempts at a Cel/Pot rush combat deck). CL does not fix the
problem of degenerate all-vote decks.

Messages.Author: Eric Pettersen
Messages.Body:
ncas...@aol.com (NCascone) wrote:
> I saw at least 1 Brujah Rush deck posted under CL. The leading NL
> proponent dismissed it because "real Brujah don't use guns". Hardly a

> definitive counterargument . . . I'll try building a Rush deck for my next
> game, and then post the results. Still, it seems like there are plenty of
> force-a-combat cards to deal with a S&B if you're not the prey. If you
> are the prey, you need to use the multi-player dynamic to get the others
> to help eliminate the Malk before they start scoring big. This has been
> cited as a negative; to me it's a matter of taste.
>

> To sum up, I think the Malk S&B situation is the biggest argument to
> playing with CL. I plan to try my hand at building a Rush deck under 4CL.
> I still think it can be done. I'm willing to be convinced, but I need
> empirical evidence that the claims against Rush combat under CL are true.
>

> Looking forward to hearing more about this . . .

You know, I play with no limits but don't care if various people want to
play with 4CL, as long as I don't have to play that way. I don't see why
you would want to use 4CL in a game that wasn't designed with them in mind
and works well without them (with some minor rule changes). Nonetheless,
I don't want to get in the middle of the 4CL vs. no limits debate.

However, I am very tired of a debate where neither side really pays
attention to what the other side says. Very little useful information is
generated this way. The classic example of this lack of communication is
the Brujah Rush thing. The NL camp never said you couldn't make a 4CL
Brujah Rush deck. What they _did_ say was that you couldn't make a 4CL
Brujah Cel/Pot deck, i.e. there was a deck type available under NL that
was impossible under 4CL.

Now a Brujah Cel/Pot deck is different from a Brujah Rush deck based on
guns in several important ways. I'm not saying which is better, but the
advantages of the Cel/Pot deck are:

The Cel/Pot vampire is ready immediately to Rush; no equipping
actions are necessary.

The Cel/Pot vampire is not vulnerable to Canine Horde, Fast Hands,
Blood Rage/Fury nor Peace Treaty.

The Cel/Pot vamp is ready to fight without expending pool on
weapons.

Now, the gun deck has other advantages, such as being able to fight under
Thoughts Betrayed, but that isn't the point. The _point_ is that the
Brujah Cel/Pot deck is unavailable under 4CL.
---
Eric Pettersen
pe...@cgl.ucsf.edu (NeXTmail capable)

Messages.Author: NCascone
Messages.Body:
In article <4culcl$r...@usenet.ucs.indiana.edu>,
aha...@bigbang.astro.indiana.edu (Alec Habig) writes:

>No, not really. It just means that you can't use a handful of PA cards
for
>your votes. You'll have to use those nice presence based plus vote
cards,
>for
>instance. Without a limit of one PA per meth, there's simply no reason
to
>ever
>use cards like Bewitching Oration. Or, for that matter, any of the other
>more
>convoluted cards that deal with voting/politics. Simply put PA cards in
the
>deck instead, they're always worth a free vote, and you can always use
them
>as an action, too!
>

Simply disagree with the above. The Pre-based voting cards and Cryptic
Rider, etc. have their places in any voting deck; especially under CL.
Extra PA's don't get replaced during the vote (Pre-based cards do), and
they only count for 1 each.

>>Calling a vote is a 1-stealth action, easily blocked. All the vote
cards in
>>the world won't help you in the ensuing combat.
>

>Quite true, but irrelevant to the question. When getting intercepted, it
>doesn't matter if you've got 8 million votes or one.
>

Hardly irrelevant. I was responding to the idea that voting needed an
outside-the-rules "fix" limiting each Meth to 1 PA per vote. Meths that
load up on PA at the expense of combat/defense cards make themselves
vulnerable to other Meths with enough intercept to block their voting
actions. To my mind, that's the non-voting deck's main counter to the
vote deck.

>>If NL needs this "fix", it seems pretty unstable . .
>

>Huh? Even under 4CL, vote pushing is king. Just put four of every PA in
>your
>deck. One's as good as another when it comes to getting more votes to
pass
>something.
>

See above.

>> ditto for repeat actions. CL fixes both these problems.
>

>Yes. Note what I said : "if you add the following two fixes ...
degenerate
>decks don't really work under NL". I simply feel that 4CL is like fixing
a
>short circuit by smashing the circuitboard with a mallet. "Look ma, no
more
>short!!" I'd much rather fix the specific problem (repeat actions) than
>change
>the way the whole game works.

OK, but this doesn't address CL's benefits to players short of cards
(players with fewer cards in my group understandably balked when I
suggested going to a NL environment), or the increased predictability (and
therefore, to me, decreased interest) in NL decks. This issue is a matter
of taste, not arguable.

>
>>I've never agreed with the concept that more cards are needed under CL.
>>Most of the "similar effect" cards are commons/uncommons anyway. Other
>>than Kine Dominance, I can't think of a rare that I regularly include in
>>my decks at the limit (plus, I only have 3 KD).
>

>Fists of Death. Flesh of Marble. Psychic Veil. And that's just off the
top
>of my head. I've never seen a DS card, so I don't know if they've done
the
>MtG thing of adding more similar cards, but it could be even worse.

FoD is an expensive way to get more hand damage. FoM's OK, but not so
much better than a dodge/additional strike, and needs Pro. Much as I want
to, I haven;t been able to use Psychic Veil as well as I thought . . . at
best, it's worth a couple of normal +1 stealth cards . . .

>
>BTW, it's looking like a fix for Thoughts Betrayed should join the above
two
>fixes. However, I've never even seen the card, so can't comment on that
:)

See, this is the problem with NL. As long as WotC does insufficient
playtesting, each expansion will contain cards that have unexpected
results in NL. In CL, the cards won't be so much of a problem. I'd
rather see an overall CL introduced than a bunch of unconnected,
cobbled-together rules designed to fix specific cards/actions, or even
limits on certain cards but not others. To me, the current tournament
rules for deck construction are unacceptable, targeting one type of deck
without addressing any other.

Messages.Body:

>Okay, one last 4cl argument that I haven't really seen addressed: in 4cl
>the fifth through fortieth extra cards aren't all that useful, and I've

>think I would have too much of an impetus to do this under no limits.

Peace T.J.,

Well, locally, we've given or offered to give various commons & some
uncommons to new players. I feel this has to do more with generosity (sp)
than having enough cards. You see a similar effect in Mt$. Since any
cards above four are "useless", some players (the generous ones) give
their dupes away. Some other players won't give land away.

> It may have been Curt Adams who wrote that and ideal number of WWEF
>can be obtained by opening only *two* booster starter boxes (pardon me
>if it isn't). This seems to be a prohibitive entrance fee to get a
>sufficient amount of *commons*, of all things...

Well, I personally disagree with Curt on the "ideal" number of WWEFs.
I have decks with four or less wakes in them (my Gangel deck has zero,
I believe). There will always be certain cards which are more desir-
able than others. It is part of the nature of the beast. At $20-30
per box of boosters, I don't think that getting enough cards to be
able to get/trade for "enough" WWEFs is all that expensive (one box
should provide enough trade fodder to get what you want).

Messages.Author: T.J. Hull
Messages.Body:
(the infamous 4cl Malk deck!)

> Sneak Cards:
> 4 Cloak the Gathering
> 4 Faceless Night
> 4 Lost in Crowds
> 4 Mask of 1000 Faces
> 4 Seduction
> 4 Spying Mission
> 4 Psychic Veil
>
> Bleed Cards
> 4 Bonding
> 4 Conditioning
> 4 Deflection
> 4 Computer Hacking
> 4 Govern the Unaligned
> 4 Kine Dominance
> 4 Threats
> 1 Pulse of the Canaille

Alright, let's look at the possibility of an intercept combat solution
to this.

Intercept Permanants: KRCG, Mr. Winthrop, Sports Bike, London Tabloid.

Advantages: offer intercept where no additional card playing is
required. Disadvantages: costs pool (except for Mr. Winthrop); one of
each would give a daunting +4 intercept, but would cost 6 pool and
take a minimum of 2 turns to set up. Two of these cards are masters,
and three are unique: but these are surmountable.

Non-permanent intercept: 2nd tradition, Elder Intervention, Telepathic
Misdirection, Spirit's Touch, Eagle's Sight, Enhanced Senses, Psychic
Projection.

Summary: 7 types of stealth cards, only one of which gives more than +1
stealth. 7 types of non-permanent intercept cards, 4 of which give +2
intercept; 4 types of permanent intercept.

There exists far,far more intercept than stealth. I suggest Masika
with a flame thrower. Of course, Protean offers 2 more types of
stealth cards, but this still does not equal the amount of intercept.

Can you give me some examples of decks which are viable under CL which
are not viable under NL?

>>>To sum up, I think the Malk S&B situation is the biggest argument to
>>>playing with CL. I plan to try my hand at building a Rush deck under
>4CL.
>>

>>Malk S&B are not hindered at all under 4cl:
>> (another posting of the 4CL Malk S&B deck, and its analysis)
>
>Understood. The multiplicity of different stealth cards let any Obf-user
>(I happen to be playing Nosferatu right now, same idea, better in combat)
>do his thing under CL and hinder other deck ideas. That's been granted.
>Let's move past restating this and get on to the next step. I'd love to
>see the NL Rush Combat deck posted, so I can start with that and adjust
>for CL.

Ok, we agree. Certain card effects: bleed mod, stealth, intercept, etc.
are "duplicated" enough so that strategies based on those effects can
remain effective under CL.

Messages.Author: T.J. Hull
Messages.Body:
Sorry about replying to my own post; my server is acting up.

Anyway: what happens if you don't catch that Malkavian?

1. Major Boon. You should Major Boon your Malkavian predator at the
earliest oppurtunity. Malkavians have great difficulty keeping blood
in their pool without killing their prey; the threat of taking a six+
point bleed themselves is usually enough to kepp them bleeding you at
three or so for a while, making it easier to catch them (since they're
jamming their own hand). Their alternative of biting the bullet and
taking one huge bleed isn't so terrible either.

2. Telepathic Misdirection; some Toreador can also use Deflection.

3. Telepathic Counter (Î often don't include this).

A note about "exercising" the Malkavian's deck; if one is playing an
intercept combat deck, your deck gets equally exercised. If you run
out of intercept, you have a perfectly good combat deck; if they run
out of stealth, their vampires simply beg to be killed. Generally, if
you want to go though your deck use KRCG, etc. last.

Finally, a crypt:

Franciscus
Dieter Kleist
Brazil
Colin Flynn
Zoe
Dorian Strack
Felicia Nostrum x2
Kallista, Master Sculptor
Masika x3

More Zoes might be good. Thanks - TJH

turn. Toss it as your predator does her last action. It never really

Most decks and players I've talked to feel WWEF is excellent. One even
goes so far as to include 4 for every deck. How does one get around
_not_ using it? Many of mine do not, but they are typically animalism
decks or supply other untappers.

Unfortunately, one can only block so many times. The main (to my mind,
the only) source of degeneracy in political decks is weenie hordling. Unless
you can reliably keep 4 minions untapped and 4 Wakes in your hand and
sufficient intercept around, the weenie hordlings are just going to
overrun. Burn all you want; there's more coming out. And vampires in
torpor even count for Autarkis Persecution, at least according to
card text. "Darn. You torpored 4 of my guys. Lessee, I'll call an
Autarkis. That's 3 guys out of torpor, 7 in...I'll gain 10 pool. Hey,
that was fun. Let's do it again. And during influence, I'll bring out
a couple three more folks."

A superior combat deck of a particular stripe can slow this deck down,
but not stop it.

>therefore, to me, decreased interest) in NL decks. This issue is a matter
>of taste, not arguable.

de gustibum non disputandum est, and all that, surely. But I must take
issue with your 'increased predictability' remark. Certainly, a given
deck becomes more predictable (once you figure out what its trick is --
which is nontrivial in some cases), but NL increases the variety of
deck *types*, which is (I believe) the argument of the NL camp.

So, instead of the uncertainty of wondering if your trick will show up
(because, under 4cl, you can't make it a sure thing), you have the
uncertainty of wondering whether this partcular trick is going to
work better than the rest of the tables' tricks. And, under NL, there
are so *many* different approaches to the same goal that it's a variety
all its own.

>FoD is an expensive way to get more hand damage. FoM's OK, but not so
>much better than a dodge/additional strike, and needs Pro. Much as I want
>to, I haven;t been able to use Psychic Veil as well as I thought . . . at
>best, it's worth a couple of normal +1 stealth cards . . .

I think what Mr. Habig was trying to point out is that these cards,
even though their effects are similar (or, in some cases, inferior) to
certain commons, the fact that you can have 8 +hand damage cards in a deck
as opposed to 4 (FoD + Undead Str vs. US alone), or 4 more stealth cards,
or 4 more prevent damage cards, or whatever, gives the edge to folks with
more rares, simply because a deck with 4 Fod & 4 US has better odds of
increasing hand damage in a given combat than a deck with only 4 US.

But if you can throw in 8 or 12 US, then the only advantage the guy with
4 or 6 FoD has is that he can stack them with US...and as you mentioned,
it costs a blood. Better to pack more (free) US and just a couple three
FoDs. The game becomes self-limiting.

>See, this is the problem with NL. As long as WotC does insufficient
>playtesting, each expansion will contain cards that have unexpected

>results in NL. In CL, the cards won't be so much of a problem.

Unfortunately (as has been pointed out by others), CL fixes the nail
that sticks up by burning the whole damn lumber yard. It's downright
Procrustean.

>I'd
>rather see an overall CL introduced than a bunch of unconnected,
>cobbled-together rules designed to fix specific cards/actions, or even

>limits on certain cards but not others.

Oy. Definitely a matter of taste. I'd much rather have a balanced
cardset, but failing that, I'm willing to swallow specific limits on some
cards.

>To me, the current tournament
>rules for deck construction are unacceptable, targeting one type of deck
>without addressing any other.

Amen. No argument from me here.

NCascone (ncas...@aol.com) wrote:
: sjoh...@math.scarolina.edu (L. Scott Johnson) writes:

: >Use Bewitching Orations, or even Charming Lobby. Besides, votes aren't
: >supposed to be sure things - they're supposed to promote table-wide
: >deals and discussions and broken promises. If you can guarantee every

: >vote will pass, that becomes more boring than S&B.

: Naturally votes aren't suposed to be sure things, but if you're building a

: vote deck, you're emphasizing that aspect of the game, hoping to be
: successful at it, at the expense of others. This is the whole idea of
: deck building, I thought. And you can still block the vote-caller with
: only 1 intercept (haven't heard anything about that yet).

The vote-caller can be blocked using only +1 intercept in _either_ CL or
NL - it isn't really something that changes between games.

It has been an observation (both of myself and of others on this group)
that there doesn't tend to be as much intercept hanging around in NL as
there does in CL. Some of the reasons for this are;

1) CL is more permanent-based. This leads to a buildup for 2 reasons:
- In CL, there are a limited number of intercept cards available to
even the Auspex-heavy clans. Becuase of this, permanents (KRCG,
Sports Bikes, London Evening Star) are needed if intercept is desired.
- Becuase permanents have a much greater role, people have an increasing
desire to stop their equipping. As an example: If Anvil equips
with a SMG in CL, that is _incredibly_ dangerous, as now I _know_
that he's going to do at least 4 damage every time, rather than have
to hope for the right cards. Under NL, Rake was likely going to
be doing at least 4-6 every turn _anyway_... Also, getting that
first Sports Bike is crucial - you can now stop your predator/prey
from getting theirs.

2) In CL, there is the 'What else am I going to put in?' factor. You only
have a limited amount of useful cards you can add from your core disciplines,
so you need other cards to fill the gaps wqhile you wait for them to
appear. The permanent (or non-permanent) intercept cards allow you to
feel like you are doing something useful.

3) Due to the lack of other ways to get into combat under CL, the Combat
decks are forced to block actions in order to do so. This means that
they need intercept.

4) Under NL, perfectly viable Auspex decks can be built without including
a single intercept card - attempting to do so under CL is basically a
waste of time.

Thus, intercept shows up more often in CL than in NL. Because of this,
there is a much more significant chance of that 'one point of intercept'
needed to block a vote _existing_ than there is under NL.

: >>I saw at least 1 Brujah Rush deck posted under CL. The leading NL

: >>proponent dismissed it because "real Brujah don't use guns".

: This is straining at a pea. If there's a viable counter-strategy to S&B
: under CL, what's the difference whether it's "Rush Combat" or
: "Vote/Rush/Gun"? Nomenclature? What's the big deal?

A valid point; you will, however, have difficulty in getting any amount of
people to agree on the definition of 'viable'. For onr person, it means
"I can stop him with the help of the table about 80% of the time," while
for another it means "If he is my predator, I should be able to survive
his attacks without anyone else's help about 50%, plus/minus luck factors
and who is the better deck-builder."

Viable is in the eye of the beholder.

: >That a table will gang up on a overly-powerful deck does not mean that

: >overly-powerful decks are a good thing.

: Wait a minute, what about those "table-wide deals and discussions and
: broken promises" you mentioned before? Those are only OK during votes?

Yes. Voting is the _one_ time during a Jyhad game where it is not only
acceptable, it is _expected_ that you will attempt to make deals and come
to aggreements in an attempt to pass/defeat a vote. It is written into
the rules that way, _deliberately_ so by the designer of the game. All
other actions (bleeding included, before the Rules Team changed the
meaning of the (D) symbol) are intended to be aimed at your prey _only_.

Voting is (originally) the only thing that can affect someone other than
your prey; therefore, voting is the only thing that should involve anyone
other than your prey in determining the success/failure of a given action.

: >Every basic strategy should have a viable deck. This is not the case
: under 4cl.

: I think you're trying to make CL more like NL here. "Rush Combat" may be
: a "basic strategy" under NL, but, as defined by the NL folks, it's "not
: viable" under CL. OK, but there are decks that become viable under CL
: that aren't in an NL environment (BTW, don't bother with the "CL is a
: subset of NL" argument, I know that).

Again, we have the word 'viable'. If you are talking about taking a CL
deck and moving it to a NL environment, then yes; that deck, as made, is
not a viable deck anymore. The _concept_, however, may still be a
workable one which needs only minor revisions in order to work.

This gets back to terminology; James asked for a cel/pot rush deck and was
given instead a vote/guns/rush deck. He indicated that this was not what
he was looking for; he wanted something which conformed _exactly_ to the
specifications he had set out. The person replying to him looked instead
at the _reasons_ for setting those conditions (to stop a Malkavian) and
instead designed a deck which had a decent chance of doing just that (in
a CL environment.) Neither proponent was happy when the other didn't
agree with them, because the challenge had _obviously_ been passed/failed...

Terminology is everything - until one agrees on the basic terms, one
cannot ever hope to agree on the results.

Saskatoon, Saskatchewan | that there is no need to do so, almost everybody

It doesn't really hurt your political deck. It just forces you to play
with more variety to be robust.

"If NL needs this 'fix'..." it does not mean that it is pretty unstable.
The fix NL gives to vote pushing is necessary in a 4CL envirnoment as
well. By putting in 4 of each of the offensive votes (for 24 damaging
votes), a few praxis seizures, and a bunch of other votes for flavor, a
4CL deck is just as hurt. You may only need one intercept to block a
vote, but the weenie-voter doesn't give a damn. You can't block the next
couple of votes. For repeated actions, the 4CL environment isn't much
better. The league I started has shown me this. I play a
presence/protean/fortitude deck (Ventrue/Gangrel, of course), and have
alot of "tapper" cards (Majesty, Earth Meld, Form of Mist, Freak Drive),
with fortitude for damage prevention. They block, they tap, I keep going
(usually). I go again. The league doesn't play with CL but nearly no
one has more than 4 of a card (though someone managed 3 gypsies). Whenever
this "tapper" effect happens (because I get a lucky series of draws), I
usually oust my prey. With 4 of each and a 80 card deck, 20% of my cards
are "tappers". I am virtually guaranteed to be tapping out my prey, and
still do what I want. There is no effective answer to this under 4CL
either. In both cases, without this errata, decks need to beef up on
"anti-S:CE" cards.

> I've never agreed with the concept that more cards are needed under CL.
> Most of the "similar effect" cards are commons/uncommons anyway. Other
> than Kine Dominance, I can't think of a rare that I regularly include in
> my decks at the limit (plus, I only have 3 KD).

Immortal Grapple for one...

> I saw at least 1 Brujah Rush deck posted under CL. The leading NL

> proponent dismissed it because "real Brujah don't use guns". Hardly a
> definitive counterargument . . . I'll try building a Rush deck for my next
> game, and then post the results. Still, it seems like there are plenty of

> force-a-combat cards to deal with a S&B if you're not the prey. If you

> are the prey, you need to use the multi-player dynamic to get the others
> to help eliminate the Malk before they start scoring big. This has been
> cited as a negative; to me it's a matter of taste.

In my opinion, no singular deck should need the agreement of the entire
table to oust it. When was the last time you played Diplomacy, or Risk,
or whatever strategy game, and said "Aha! They are playing Blue!!! We
must gang up on them or we will all be devoured (or at least lose)." It
doesn't happen, because in those games, you gang up on someone when
someone has become a threat in regards to their position (i.e., they have
too much territory) instead of who they are (they are blue). In
_non-trivial_ games, any of the offered strategies should have some merit
and there should not exist a strategy that is penultimate. The fun of
playing Diplomacy is that winning the game comes from variance on
strategy, not saying "I won, even though I wasn't playing Turkey."
This statement should not happen in a non-trivial game.

> To sum up, I think the Malk S&B situation is the biggest argument to
> playing with CL.

I'm not sure if I understand what you mean. Malk S&B under 4CL shows no
other strong rivals. A 4CL Malk S&B deck can hang with most NL playing
groups. I have never seen it cited as a reason _for_ CL. What is your?

> I plan to try my hand at building a Rush deck under 4CL.
> I still think it can be done. I'm willing to be convinced, but I need
> empirical evidence that the claims against Rush combat under CL are true.

I hope you do well.

> Looking forward to hearing more about this . . .

In this group, I'm sure you will... :)

There are several permanent stealth things, too - also, did you include
Bonding in your stealth count?

Overall, cardwise, stealth and intercept are reasonably balanced. Throw in the
fact that many actions are at a natural +1 stealth, things become a little more
difficult.

"But!", you exclaim, "the most important action, bleeding, is at no
natural stealth!". Quite true. However, this highlights the main problem :

Stealthing bleeds contributes directly to your victory condition - oust your
prey. Intercept is primarily defensive. Loading up on intercept might save
you from your predator, but does little to help you oust your own prey. A
maxed out intercept deck will probobly stalemate vs. a S&B deck predator. But,
it does nothing vs. anybody else. OtoH, that S&B deck beats anybody except
that maxed out intercept deck, and perhaps a weenie vote deck. Therein lies
the Big Imbalance.

No, this isn't "actually" a problem with playtesting; there's a problem
there _as_well_. But _because_ there's a problem there, NL will continue
to need more and more card-specified rules. Now it looks like Toreador
Grand Ball is also broken . . .

>4CL will restrict the spoiler cards, but has the miserable side effect
>of restricting good, balanced cards as well.

"Miserable" . . . value-loaded words are almost always a matter of taste.

>>rather see an overall CL introduced than a bunch of unconnected,
>>cobbled-together rules designed to fix specific cards/actions, or even
>

Yeah, let's continue to have lousy playtesting. That's what I want.

>>limits on certain cards but not others. To me, the current tournament
>>rules for deck construction are unacceptable, targeting one type of deck
>>without addressing any other.
>

>Agreed wholeheartedly.

Hooray!

Look, here's my current position. NL needs fixes on specific
cards/actions because of insufficient playtesting, an issue about which we
can do nothing. It makes possible decks that are OTP's, which are dull to
play against. It rewards people who have loads of expensive cards to put
in their decks.

CL helps address the broken-card/action issue by limiting their frequency.
It's more difficult to make a OTP (except the S&B). In my experience,
people who have fewer cards are more comfortable with a CL environment
because they feel less threatened.

The main argument against CL right now is that it maks the S&B deck a
stable strategy by "eliminating" the effectiveness of it's natural enemy,
the Rush combat deck. I believe the jury is still out on this question.

Also, please note: while 4CL may be too restrictive for the Rush deck,
perhaps 8CL or 15% would allow it to work. This is a question that can be
resolved _in_play_; CL fans should get on it. I am.

Messages.Author: CurtAdams
Messages.Body:
"James R. McClure Jr." <jmcc...@e-mail.kdp-baptist.louisville.edu>
writes:

>curt...@aol.com (CurtAdams) wrote:

>>It's true that players with small collections who do not trade are at a
>>disadvantage in a NL game.
^^^^
>Change this to "any trading card" and you have a true statement.

Oh, absolutely. Actually, it should come as no surprise that people who
don't (or can't) trade are at a big disadvantage in a trading card game.

Jyhad, however, has relatively strong categorization, by which I mean
cards fall into categories (particular disciplines, clans, or strategies).
Cards out of your deck's categories are generally completely useless, and
often actively detrimental due to immediate redraw and limited discard.
Since there are so many categories, most Jyhad cards are quite useless in
any given deck. So it's actually harder to build a playable deck out of a
small *untraded* card set in Jyhad than in most other CCGs.

The flip side is that since rares are not particularly useful you can
trade away rares to get the commons you need. So if you trade, you can
make a really good deck (often tournament-caliber) from a small card
collection.

NL Jyhad, then, is more of a *trading* card game than anything else on the
market.

If you go to 4cl, the overall power level drops, assuming you control the
Malks with gentlevampire's agreements or table gangup policies or some
such. So it is easier to design a playable deck without trading. At the
same time, it becomes harder to design a really competitive deck, because
you've got to have particular rares to substitute for the extra commons
you're no longer allowed (e.g., Kine Dominance for Bonding, Fists of Death
for Undead Strength, etc.)

IMO, the best policy is to go NL and trade. That way you can get really
good decks -not just playable ones - with small collections. If somebody
finds trading unpleasant and isn't willing or able to become a suitcase
player, Jyhad really isn't the game for them.

>Players

certain

>problem is aggravated.

Others have mentioned this, but I too usually mean any limit when I mean
CL. I used to be in the 10% camp myself. As most people arguing for
limits seem to be in the 4CL camp, I usually tend to address my responses
with that in mind. I guess I am guilty of 4cardism (a close relative to
the other -isms :).

Most of my deck would conform to a 10% limit. The problem for me in
_enforcing_ such a limit, is that it is not a necessary one. Why do it?
Most decks that are made NL are ~ 10% limit. Those that are not made by
it, so what? IMHO, One simply cannot create a "degenerate" deck under
NL, so why add a limit to a game that wasn't designed with one in mind?
As Curt mentioned earlier, once you put in your 20th card of ultimate
doom, you begin to not be able to do _anything_. So what if you have a
KRC? You need the votes to pass it (as long as you are not playing
unlimited vote push), you may need stealth. You will still need
defensive cards.

My transformation from 6CL(3 weeks) -> 10% happened because I tried it,
liked it and found no ill result. My transformation from 10% (2 months)
-> NL happened because I realised that they were virtually identical, and
that with a few house rules, what could one do in NL? No more than any
other deck. Whatever people believe about Jyhad (or for that matter,
anything), it is always best to question your opinions, and if possible
test them. Wherever you arrive, even if it is the same place, you are
always better for it. (Imagine, kids, for only a modest hourly fee or a
little tuition, you too can be privy to the secrets of the universe! :)

Not quite. Rares that are powerful are typically unique or highly
expensive (a la horrid reality) or both. For the remainder, it is not
the rares that are need in bulk, but the commons - the Bum's Rushes, the
Telepathic Counters, etc.. On the contrary, a CL environment rewards
people who have loads of expensive cards because after they max out on
torn signposts they can go to town with fists of death.

CL also needs fixes on the "broken card" issue, or at least as much as NL
does. As an example, look at LSJ's house rules. Nearly all of them
could be taken away and NL holds. All you need to hang on to are
these:

@#$@#$ The "Golden Tenents" of Jyhad $#@$#@
1) No unlimited vote push
2) No repeat actions.

The rest are all flavor. Someone doesn't like what, say, Seduction does
(a (D) targeted at a player rather than a name), so they change it.
Many of the changes for cards like Majesty/Earth Meld are all the same, they
cling to the "Golden Tenents".

This is not a "bulk" of rules to carry about.

Now pretend we are in a CL environment. Suddenly, as more cards are
printed, we get the "magic" response. "You mean I can only put so many
in? I'll max out." You can see this again and again in Type I decks in
Magic. Playing black? You always throw in a Demonic Tutor. Red ->
Fork. Green -> Channel. White -> Balance. Blue -> Recall. Moxes and
Lotus to those that have them. Feldon's Cane. Sol Ring. "Ok, now let's
build the rest of the deck." In _any_ environment, if a card is "broken"
it will bring about this effect.

> CL helps address the broken-card/action issue by limiting their frequency.

> It's more difficult to make a OTP (except the S&B). In my experience,

> people who have fewer cards are more comfortable with a CL environment
> because they feel less threatened.

They do tend to feel more threatened until you show them a collection.
After they've played about 4-5 games, they can see, as cool as Patagia
is, Bum's Rush is usually more useful in their Nosferatu deck. As is
Storm Sewers.

As for CL limiting the frequency of cards, as more cards get made, CL
begins to fail at this, due to the "Lightning Bolt" effect from Magic. I
don't mean just varied forms of stealth. I mean suddenly having 4 more
S:CE or similar card usable by presence. I mean another KRC-like vote.

As an aside, see what Carlotta Giovanni (7-Blood from DS who can retrieve
_any_ card from the ash heap at 1-stealth) does in a CL environment.
Suddenly you have unlimited KRC/majesty/whatever. (Yes, she can be
blocked, but in a deck that uses her, who cares? If you play to protect
her, it doesn't matter.)

> The main argument against CL right now is that it maks the S&B deck a
> stable strategy by "eliminating" the effectiveness of it's natural enemy,
> the Rush combat deck. I believe the jury is still out on this question.

This one is too easy to demonstrate. Play a game with people you don't
know. Ask them to play 4CL (if they don't). Play the "Penultimate" S&B
deck. I would wager a lot that either it gets ganged by the table or wins
handily.

Now, give the deck to any of them, pull out you 4CL deck and be their
prey with a 4CL Limbaugh deck (Rush... I mean :). You can thoroughly
expect a grinding unless the table helps again.

W/o limits a Malk is the same as a 4CL Malk, and a Rush deck will have
some hard work to neuter the Malk. As most people concede, a 4CL deck
will not usually be able to accomplish a particular goal
(vote/combat/etc) as well (note this concession below) as a NL deck. If
the NL Rush deck has a problem, how will a 4CL fare?

> Also, please note: while 4CL may be too restrictive for the Rush deck,
> perhaps 8CL or 15% would allow it to work. This is a question that can be
> resolved _in_play_; CL fans should get on it. I am.

Glad to hear it. :) Good luck in your quest.

I don't know about his group, but we don't have a problem with Malk S&B.
And we hardly have to "gang up" against it. This is, of course, after I
showed them all what a single deck can do to Malks (my "Anson and his
Brujah Friends" deck; and LionRAR's Gangrel Intercept deck seems to hold
its own against them alright also). My deck wasn't specifically designed
to destroy Malks, but it is definitely strengthened when they are on the
table! Like when I Malk Dementia his Duane and then Golconda his butt.
Yum! Or MD his Ozmo, Minion Tap him to 1 blood, and then send him into
Trapped combat against my Prey (the Prey usually elects not to take the
bleed). Anyone want to diablarize? I'm not blocking! Even without
Anson out, stealing Ozmo and sending him in to bleed my prey is a good
thing, as it's a no-lose situation. At the very least, he's out of my
hair for a little while. I particularly liked stealing the Malk IC
member from my Predator. Note that this isn't just a "Malk-Nuke" deck,
but a deck that stands well on it's own (having an estimated 60/40 win/loss
ratio when either Anson doesn't come out or there are no Malks on the
table); however, if there *are* Malks out there, this deck actually
increases in strength.

Aside from MD's though, which are admittedly a Malk-specific card, I also
like Archon Investigations, which I have used to before to burn, for
example, Democritus (a highlight in my Jyhad career ;) ). At the very
least, just the threat of them in your prey's hand tends to slow down the
bleed modifications.

It seems to me that the opponents of 4CL are leaving out the V:TES cards,
either because they don't have them (Peace, James, as I know this is the
case with you) or they are just ignoring them. For example, a Pot/Cel
Rush deck is IMHO very viable under 4CL, particularly after you include
some of the new cards (Volker and Rake will allow you to ust play little
vamps and still be able to use Bloodhunts (even better than Bum's Rushes
in certain instances, as they last longer than a turn, and better than
Haven Uncovereds, as they can't re SRed or later removed, and they don't
take a Master Phase Action). I will be modifying James' Cel/Pot Rush
Deck, and trying to get someone else to play a Malk S&B deck (modified
from one I downloaded to make it even more sick), to see how the Rush
deck fares under 4CL.

>My original question was,
>"Are there any CL deck ideas/concepts/themes which will _not_ work under NL?"
>There are NL i/c/t which don't work under CL.

So name one, besides Cel/Pot Rush (a myth that I and others are working
to dispel). IMHO 4CL works well to slow down "selfish vote" decks (sure,
you can throw in other PAs to push votes, but it's far *better* to only
put in KRCs and a few Conservative Agitations), and Malk S&B decks aren't
any more of a problem than Gangrel "Intercept&Burn" (which seem to give
me the most problem). And 4CL does this with one simple house rule, as
opposed to multiple house rules and/or a limited list. If you can't come
up with a good way to counter a deck, IMHO it's because you haven't tried
hard enough (just from reading your posts, I can tell that you are all
*smart* enough, you just don't seem to be giving it a chance).

Some arguments I have read say "Why an artificial 4-card limit?"
Artificial? *All* the rules are artificial, in that they were
constructed; they didn't just fall from the sky. Why not a 4-card limit
(as opposed to another CL)? So it has the stigma of Tragic:TG attached
to it. Is this so bad? IMHO a 3-card limit is too limiting, and a 6-card
limit (in a typical 80-90 card deck) does very little to limit *anything*
(the NL deck examples that I have seen don't seem to use more than 6 of
any but 1 or two cards, and those 1 or 2 cards are only present in
numbers like 7 or 8). Maybe a 5-card limit is best, but if I take this
to my play group, I know they will ask, "Why a 5-card limit?" Why? I
don't know. Because 4CL is too much like Magic?

Messages.Author: Scott A DiBerardino
Messages.Body:
I've been following the CL vs NL debate for awhile. I've tried both. I've
tried *really* restricted play (4CL plus no duplicate Masters!), and I've
tried no-holds-barred NL with an extensive collection. I had fun both
ways, but...

On the NL side, I can understand and agree all the logical arguments
against card limites, particularly how it affects the level of power of
permanents in the game. To me, this is the strongest argument.

However, on the CL side, I've become disgusted with the NL environment
because once players (new ones) got over their magic-mindset, the decks
and play got extremely *boring*. A deck made out of (essentially) four to
six cards just gets boring after a couple turns.

I think the main difference between the two camps is that CL players are
looking for a good *game*, while NL players are looking for a good gaming
*environment*. I have to admit that each individual *game* under CL was
more fun, but that NL opened up more possibilities... but games were often
lopsided and dull.

I've considered my own feelings on this subject for weeks now, and the
only compromise (and I have to admit, I feel one is necessary) is:
well, either play with no limits and avoid "boring" players (a problem in
that often one finds this out too late), or play with some loose limits
(6CL, 10% whatever) but allow one or two cards to "break the rule"... just
name your transgressing card (usually Rush), and away you go! It's an idea
anyway, mainly to promote within-game variety.

Just had to let out my recent thoughts. You may return to your pointless
bickering. :)

-scott

-- Monsieur de Saint-Savin, _The_Island_of_the_Day_Before_

Throw in Presence Based Bleed and Misdirection and your deck is
finished. With Skill cards, you find yourself with 16 Masters, a base
deck of 40 cards and you throw in Presence bleed for fun. When my own
deck has come up with its multitude of untap, only rules disallowing
repeat actions have allowed me to swarm my prey. As a result, I have
thrown in offensive vote to keep up the pressure. On a side note, if
a decent interceptor can't get up next to a deck with Carlotta Giovanni,
that deck has effectively won (each time I have seen Carlotta come up in
the Brujah/Giovanni Brute Force Politics deck, KRC every turn..., without
others having a decent reliable way to stop it.) CL does not address
these.

As for the true "bear": vote push. In _ANY_ environment, weenie vote push
reigns supreme. Here is an explicit example:

@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$

The Battle Royal: A Weenie 4CL Vote Push Deck vs. Five Other NL Decks

I was playing Jyhad one night with an experiment in mind. I had played
with vote pushing before, but had never seen it actually done to the
edge. Would it still work under 4CL? See for yourself.

The five other decks are my own. Others who have played them or
agaisnt them might attest by their integrity as decks (I certainly do).
They are all constructed under NL, and I'm sure that even the CL-camp
will agree: a NL deck can more easily accomplish an objective than a CL
deck. I.e., NL Rush is more reliable, etc..

The Decks, in order of play:

1) "The Slumlords": A Nosferatu Political deck. Rush/Hidden
Lurker the other voters. Pass your own at will. Only uses POT/OBF.
2) "Jeute! Merde!": A Ravnos "Screw" deck. Has all of the
clan/strategy hosers. It uses thievery, Sudden Reversals, and Cross
Table Stealth Reduction to mess with the table. Much anti-politics.
3) "Sowing Dissension's Seeds": A Presence Based Politics deck.
Uses 2 Haven Uncovered and 6 Bloodhunts to get the table to fight
itself. Dramatic Upheavels to move about to the best location. VERY
good at making a vampire targetable.
4) "WEENIE VOTE PUSH": See below.
5) "The Stoic": A Gangrel Permanent Intercept deck. Regularly
gets several minions with +1, and one with +3, not including cat's
guidance. Fortitude combat and mucho presses.
6) "It Runs Like Water": A Tremere/Brujah CEL/THA deck. Uses 8
Haven Uncovered to slam dance someone by multiple attackers if
necessary. Lots of temporary intercept, Bleed Bounce, and Cryptic Missions.

THE WEENIE VOTE PUSH DECK:
Crypt:
Two of Each Caitiff, One of each other 2-Capacity, One Gideon Fontaine.

Library:
4 Misdirection, 4 Anarch Revolt, 4 Information Superhighway, 4 Effective
Management, 1 Of Each Praxis Seizure (19 Total), 4 KRC, 4 Sabbat Threat,
4 Parity Shift, 4 Conservative Agitation, 4 Domain Challenge, 4 Ancilla
Empowerment, 4 The First Tradition, 4 Regaining the Upper Hand, 4
Consainguineas (sp?) Condemnation, 4 Bewitching Oration, 2 Kindred
Segregation, 1 Command of the Harpies.
78 Card Total.

Turns: Action:
2 First Praxis Seizure called and passed with 5 pushes. Would not
have passed without pushes. Two more votes called to make another
Prince and to use Conservative Agitation, not requiring vote push.
3 Another Prince. Comprehension dawns on the table, and they begin
dealing to squash the deck.
4 The Gang Bang begins...
6 Player 2 dies
7 Player 1 dies
8 Player 6 dies
9 Player 5 decides to oust player 4 so that at least he can pick up
some victory points.
10 Player 5 dies
End result:
Weenie Vote Push Deck has 5 victory points, 11 pool, 5 vampires in
torpor, and 6 vampires in play (5 are Princes).

Without ending vote push, this will be a creatable, virtually unbeatable
deck. This deck also contested two vampires. It dropped them. Why
should it care? There is always another prince 2 pool away.

@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$@#$
One of the arguements for CL is that it does not need "bulky,
non-elegant" rules to play well. Unfortunately, this is not the case.
It _does_ need a no vote-push rule to be a viable game. Otherwise, what
then? If a new player comes with their deck will you tell them, "So
sorry, but you cannot play that deck, we just can't beat it." With
repeat actions, though I have not explicitly shown so, it to is not truly
"fixed", merely partially restrained. To top it off: Carlotta Giovanni.
Her powers make her an instant add to a deck that wants to be
"degenerate" in CL.

Whatever you argue about CL, one thing that cannot be argued is that it
does not need "inelegant" fixes. It needs them just as NL does.

>elegance. Elegance: _1a._ grace and refinement in appearance, movement, or
>manners. _b._ tasteful opulence in form, decoration, or presentation. _2a._
>grace and restraint of style. _b._ scientific precision and exactness. _3._

>for "elegant." How can you say a limit on every card, not just the problem
>ones, is "restrained of style" or "precise/exact"? This is one of the big
>problems I have with CL. It arbitrarily limits cards which aren't broken
>(even in large numbers). Why limit all the cards when only a handful are
>broken/problem cards? Since when are "sledgehammer solutions" elegant?

If I may interject a couple things here: "Elegant" in reference to game

design usually refers to the most important rule of thumb--KISS (Keep It
Simple, Stupid). If a single rule can be made that adequately solves a
game problem or loophole (or even better, a group of problems, as in this
case), it is better to use it than to use 2-3 rules
(even if the 2-3 rules might solve the problem a little better--a very
arguable point in the case of Jyhad/V:TES). A simple card limit rule is
more "elegant" in this case because it fixes the problem of the "broken"
cards with a single rule. If you play NL, you need either 2 houserules
(no repeat sactins, and no vote pushing), or a list of restricted cards,
to make the game work. And neither of these NL "fixes" address the
problems with the new cards (I know you don't use DS James, but many of
us do).

As new expansions come out, the NL playgroups will either have to adopt

new house rules to fix problems, or add to their "restricted list"
(depending upon which "fix" they use). OTOH, the groups like ours who use
CL won't have to change our play environment at all. THAT'S why CL is
more elegant.

-Elfholme

T.J. Hull (t...@nwlink.com) wrote:
: "James R. McClure Jr." <jmcc...@e-mail.kdp-baptist.louisville.edu>

: >>>There are NL i/c/t which don't work under CL.
: >>
: >>So name one, besides Cel/Pot Rush (a myth that I and others are working
: >>to dispel).
: >
: >A "Kitchen Sink" deck. That is, a deck who's primary purpose is combat
: >involving thrown objects (Sewer Lids, Cars, Gates).

: Gee, if you add ANI you suddenly have a bunch more similar strikes. A
: little creativity will get you Grenades.

Let's take an analogy of wheels. I want to be able to take one wheel and
make a unicycle, 2 wheels and make a bike, 3 wheels and make a tricycle, 4
wheels and make a car, 6 wheels and make an ATV, or 18 wheels and make a
tractor-trailer. All will get me where I want to go, but all have
trade-offs between number of passengers, gas consumption, cargo, driver
protection in case of crash, etc.

Your response to this desire is: "So you are limited to two wheels - get
creative and make a motorcycle! It will still get you where you want to
go..." Yes, it will, sort of. But why should I be limited to the
options available for motorcycles?

To bring it back to the comment you made, why should it be _necessary_ to
add animalism to make a deck concept work when all the components already
exist under a different discipline? In fact, I should be able to make an
ANI 'pitch deck' and put it up against a POT 'pitch deck' and see who
comes out on top - not be forced to rely on some bastard hybrid of the
two...

: >Unfortunately (for your argument), Jyhad was designed with the problems that

: >Tragic exposed in mind. It was designed to be fully playable without any
: >card limits.

: So was Magic.

Magic was first, and made a helluva lot of mistakes - the primary one
being that the designer cound not conceive of people spending thousands
of dollars on gaming cards. The card limits were inherent in the rarity
of cards - better cards were made rarer in the (mistaken) belief that no

I can see where you guys are coming from with the "Keep it Simple" school of
elegance.

However, let me analyze this a step further :

The NL "Golden Rule" school of fixing broken rules :

1) No repeat actions on untaps;
2) No more than 1 vote push;

Two things. Each fixes a class of problems rather than a specific card. No
matter how many "lightning bolt" style cards WotC decides to put in future
expansions, these classes of problems remain fixed.

The problem - what to do when WotC blows it and releases a card allowing for a
brand new abuse - TB may be of this ilk. So, the two rules changes may have to
grow.

The CL camp likes to think that it has one rule to fix the problem. One is
simpler than two, of course.

However, I point out that you've essentially got a 270+ card long restricted
list. One could say that this is a very complicated rule :)

As for expansions causing things to get more complicated, this is gaurenteed to
happen, given the much talked about example of the Lightning Bolt from MtG.

>>The vote pushing problem is a separate issue. I'll choose to play the game
>>as Jyhad was originally written (a meth may play _a_ PA for a vote), and
>>happily ignore VtES and the RT :)
>
>Can't find this. Quote, please?

Uhh, I don't have my Jyhad rules manual here at work, but if you own one, read
the sentence about playing PA cards for votes.

Oh, one thing on the economics of the game that I haven't seen mentioned yet.
A card limit makes commons pretty much worthless in trading. Sure, this can
result in a player giving away his 5th through 10th dupes of a card. However,
when's the last time you gave someone a number of commons for a rare in Magic?
They've got all the commons, who needs 4? If you're a new player, you've got
no options to get a neat rare for flavor, other than give up one of your own
rares.

Alan Kwan <kw...@cs.cornell.edu> wrote:

Warning: article disputes official rulings

[...]

Could it be possible that it was intended that each Methselah
can get only one vote from Political cards during each vote?

Let's try to see if this interpretation (3) contradicts with
the preceeding statement:

Assumption:
Each Methselah can get only one vote from Political cards
during each vote.

Statement:
"Additional political cards can also be used by any of the other
Methselahs for votes."

Combine:
"Additional political cards can also be used by any of the other
Methselahs for votes, but each Methselah can play only one such
card."

- interpretation (3)

It reads alright. The plural in "cards", under this interpretation,
refer to a total of a plural number of cards being used by a plural
number of Methselahs.

Back to the first statement:
"A political card always provides one vote for the Methselah playing
it."

"A politcal card" providing one vote. Not "each" political card.
So interpretation (3) does not contradict here, either. One possible
paraphase (according to WotC rules-editing standards):

"A Methselah gets one vote by playing a political card."

This may well be what the sentence intended to say, without the
"each" overtone.

If the limitation of only one political card being useable by each
Methselah was intended, this would explain the use of the
term "any of the _other_ Methselah", because of the (albeit
not totally correct) assumption that the calling Methselah has
already played one card.

This interpretation would also balance the fact that (as suggested
by some of the net.personality; unofficial) only one of each type of
reaction (such as Dread Gaze and Surprise Influence) can be used
during a vote, while multiple political action cards can be used.

>environment) were flawed and that is why NL Magic does not work.

To be more precise, Magic WAS designed with a card limit. Cards were
supposed to be limited by availability - no group was expected to get more
than 2000 cards, which is about 10 of each common. So there was not
supposed to be any way to build seriously degenerate decks - the cards
wouldn't be there.

When they discovered individuals were buying thousands of cards, they
threw on the 4cl to attempt to simulate the originally planned-for
situation.

Not agreed.

First, the vote pushing GT is simply the way the game was originally written.
I don't consider ignoring a misguided Rules Team ruling to be muddling at
all :)

The "no repeat actions" GT affects only several cards, seems to be a logical
clarification, and only really thumps decks that are trying to exploit the hole
in the rules.

works against any number of non-abusive deck designs.

other. If you want to use the 4CL house rule to change the deck construction
mechanics, fine. But don't try to tell me that this is somehow less of a rules
change than disallowing repeat actions.

We called and sent email and were told that we would be on the playtesting
squad, and promptly heard nothing again.

touch it was deep in the thick of the VtES planning, but if you really are

playtesting a lot.

rather bewildered that there seemed to be a lack of desire on WoTC's part
to seriously take advantage of a playtesting group. We could understand

playtesting at the time, or if we had been told that. But that wasn't
what we were told, so to us it just looked like someone dropped the ball,
or didn't care.

wonders for the stability of a great game. Players won't offer to playtest

Actually, two of the decks were intercept heavy. All of the deck at the
table were chosen by me as decks that would stand an excellent chance
against the deck.

Prey: A permanent intercept deck (only needing +1, really) with lots of
untap ability in the form of cat's guidance, homonculous, Freak Drive,
The Beast Lord, etc. I felt that its untap would keep it going.

Grand Prey: A temporary intercept and haven uncovered Cel/Tha deck. It
doesn't go big on intercept because it only wants to block at +1/+2.
When a S&B comes around it deflects/ Havens them. In this game, I felt
the direct combat and light intercept would help.

Great Grand Prey: A Rush & Politics deck. The rush should kill the
weenies. The Politics should make the pushing harder.

Grand Predator: A "Screw" Deck. It attempts to screw typical strategies
and clans. It includes a large number of anti-voting cards, and due to
the potpouri of weenies from all the clans, the anti clan cards can
always hit that deck.

Predator: A Presence Vote Deck. It easily gets the votes out. It still
didn't have enough.

I guess my whole point is that I _tried_ to throw a good selection of
decks against it (to simulate a typical game) but I warped my selection
and their placement to make things more difficult for the Weenie Vote
deck to win. The table didn't really get the idea until the third turn,
and then the table decided to go after it en masse. They torped (I
think) five vampires, all princes, but it didn't matter.

I think that the deck showed how w/o Vote Push limitations, any
environment is a broken environment.

(Pardon the tardiness or many of my responses lately, especially in the
CL/NCL debate. My server has been feeding me articles on a 24-48 hour+
delay for the last while... :-(

Elegant is another one of those 'eye of the beholder' words (obviously)
in which many different people can have widelt differing opinions. As
for me, however, I perceive elegance in things which are: precise (rather
than general), understated (rather than overplayed), sleek, and use only
as much force/effort/action/thought as necessary.

Examples:
- An equation which takes three boards of calculations to come to a
conclusion is not as elegant as an equation which takes only 15 lines.
- Two martial artists fighting can be elegant, as they (theoretically)
apply the minimum necessary force at precisely defined locations to
achieve the desired result. Two guys bare-knuckle fighting in the corner
of a bar is (usually) not elegant, _even though_ the result is the same:
one guy wins and the other loses.
- If one person in a classroom is having trouble with binomial equations,
it is not an 'elegant' solution to assign extra homework for everyone.
This solution targets not only those who are a problem, but also those
who aren't. As a result, those who _are_ having difficulty _still_ may
not get the attention they need.

Elegance comes _through_ hard work, not by avoiding it. Fred Astaire
looks elegant when he dances because he has put in many hours practicing,
trying things out, knowing what works and what doesn't. Similarly for the
Martial Artists - they can only achieve their elegance through knowledge
and practice. It is far easier to say 'everybody do questions XX on page
X' than to look and determine who really needs the help. The 3-board
equation _works_, and still solves the problem, but it is usually a 'first
pass'; it is a basis from one works to _achieve_ elegance, not elegance
itself.

How does this apply to the CL/NCL debate? In this way:

The 4CL is indeed 'simpler' than targetted solutions; as a 'first pass'
it does the job acceptably with a minimum of fuss, much in the same way
that breaking a table over someone's head will cause them to lose
consciousness - effective, but not elegant.

The specific House Rules on broken cards are an effort to try and apply
force _only where necessary_, and not as a blanket solution. While they
do work (at least, some combination of them usually does the trick) they
fall down where the 'simplicity' factor kicks in. There is no denying
that it _is_ more difficult to remember many rules than to remember one;
it is also more difficult to do something well than to do it poorly, but
that _in and of itself_ is not a reason for doing it poorly.

The 'Golden Tenets' are (so far) the ultimate in elegance. They look at
an overall _class_ of problems and fix them in a way that is, while a
little sloppier than targetted rules, acceptable to all. As for
simplicity, two rules are not significantly more difficult to remember
than one and they pass this test as well.

Given, people will say that there are cards which are still broken which
are not fixed by these two rules. This means that the cycle will have to
start again - but hopefully not from scratch. Jut because a specific
vehicular design doesn't work, the engineers don't go back and reinvent
the wheel! They start from where it last _did_ work. The 'Golden Tenets'
are the last place where things did work; no blanket limits were necessary
and every card was accounted for.

The new cards will probably go through (are going through, even as we
watch!) the same discussion processes which brought about the Golden
Tenets. If that results in adding another blanket rule to the GTs to
cover a class of cards, or even if it results in a specific ruling to fix
a specific broken card - it is still better than a table over the head. :-)

> This solution targets not only those who are a problem, but also those
> who aren't. As a result, those who _are_ having difficulty _still_ may
> not get the attention they need.

An argument against a card limit...

I won't try to debate the arguments above (though I might point out that
if several of the students in the class were having problems, it *might*
be more appropriate to assign extra homework to the class...particularly
if you only have a certain amount of time to allocate to each student).
The question is, which is more important to you. You, obviously, favor
that answers be precise rather than use the minimum thought necessary. I
favor the latter. My group plays in a room provided by a game store, and
anyone is invited to stop by and play with us. It is much easier for
"drop-ins" if we play with as few house rules as possible.

<discussion of elegance coming through hard work deleted>

I'm not sure which side has put more "hard work" into their fix...but
I'll tell you this: if I started seeing a game as work, then I'd stop
playing. "Hard work" implies that you are striving against something. I
hardly think playing a game over and over (even if you are trying new
things constantly) is "hard work". Again, if you see the game as hard
work, maybe you should find something more pleasurable to spend your free
time on.

>How does this apply to the CL/NCL debate? In this way:
>
>The 4CL is indeed 'simpler' than targetted solutions; as a 'first pass'
>it does the job acceptably with a minimum of fuss, much in the same way
>that breaking a table over someone's head will cause them to lose
>consciousness - effective, but not elegant.

As more and more expansions come out for V:TES, your list of house rules
will be forced to grow (broken cards are inevitable...they are a problem
with every game, not just games produced by WOTC...though they are more
of a problem in some games than others). Eventually, I will reach the
point where I'd *rather* have a table broken over my head than remember a
bunch of rules that essentially create a different game. Whatever you
think about CL, it should be apparent that they change the rules of the
game a lot less than inventing new rules. This will become even more
apparent as more house rules become necessary to make a NL environment work.

>The specific House Rules on broken cards are an effort to try and apply
>force _only where necessary_, and not as a blanket solution. While they
>do work (at least, some combination of them usually does the trick) they
>fall down where the 'simplicity' factor kicks in. There is no denying
>that it _is_ more difficult to remember many rules than to remember one;
>it is also more difficult to do something well than to do it poorly, but
>that _in and of itself_ is not a reason for doing it poorly.

Well/poorly, that's a matter of opinion, and I don't think it's relevant
here (I think the CL solution fixes V:TES' problems just as well as the
Golden Tenets). It's also more difficult to wring stones for juice than
oranges, but is that a good reason to drink "stone juice" each morning
instead of orange juice? No.

>The 'Golden Tenets' are (so far) the ultimate in elegance. They look at
>an overall _class_ of problems and fix them in a way that is, while a
>little sloppier than targetted rules, acceptable to all. As for
>simplicity, two rules are not significantly more difficult to remember
>than one and they pass this test as well.

This is not true, even by your definition. Since you haven't assigned
"weights" to your four "factors" of elegance, a fix that is better in one
factor (precision) but worse in another (level of thought/work necessary)
is no better than the fix you are comparing it to.

>Given, people will say that there are cards which are still broken which
>are not fixed by these two rules. This means that the cycle will have to
>start again - but hopefully not from scratch. Jut because a specific
>vehicular design doesn't work, the engineers don't go back and reinvent
>the wheel! They start from where it last _did_ work. The 'Golden Tenets'
>are the last place where things did work; no blanket limits were necessary
>and every card was accounted for.

Exactly my point. Your list of rules to fix the problem will continue to
grow and get more and more complicated, while mine stays the same.

(NCascone) wrote:

> In article <4e5fp4$s...@newsbf02.news.aol.com>, curt...@aol.com
> (CurtAdams) writes:
>
> >I'm not exactly sure what you mean by mechanics here, but the two "Golden
> >Rules" have little effect other than to bar two very specific types of
> >clearly abusive decks.
>
> Actually, in addition to barring the degenerate decks, the GT's limit the
> effectiveness of untapping and voting in non-denegerate decks as well.
> This makes both of those actions less effective in the overall
> environment; a collateral effect that is more objectionable, to me, than
> playing with a loose (5 or 6) or even tight (4) CL.

One doesn't have to untap and do nothing. The GT's limit makes an
untapper deck have to be diverse (something I would think that the
CL-camp would like). Rather than being able to call 2 votes with the
same vampire, you might get a gun, call a vote, and then Force of Will to
bleed at a bonus. Following that, Movement of the Slow Body, Rapid
Healing, Restoration. This (or something similar) has happened a number
of times in our games under the GTs. Also common is the blocked KRC,
Majesty, Presence bleed. What do you want to do? Vote and Vote? Bleed
and bleed? This is possible, but even in CL (especially lose ones), this
can approach degeneracy. When it doesn't hit degeneracy it is only
because it is of slight order of magnitude less.

> >Tight card limits quite profoundly alter the game,
> >not just by the advantages to S&B, but also by heavy emphasis on
> intercept
> >and permanents and the downgrading of most disciplines.
>
> The change is just different, not better or worse. IME, it leads to more
> contestation of permanent retainers and locations, which means more play
> decisions to make.

But it also limits _choice_. It is a different, and in the terms you
presented, it is a difference of tast, but outside of your statements, it
means a limit to what a person can choose to create.

> >It also alters
> >deck construction from a focus on frequency tuning and opponent matching
> >to a substitute hunt and largely squelches trading between different
> >rarities.
>
> I'm not sure what you mean by opponent matching. If you're trying to make
> a very focused deck, CL deck construction can become a substitute hunt;
> then you get to do the frequency tuning you referred to.

Frequency tuning means to weigh in the advantages and disadvantages of
having 8 Deflections versus 3 Deflections and 5 Telepathic Misdirections,
or 6 Bum's Rush vs. 1 Bum's Rush and 5 Haven Uncovered. CL greatly bogs
this down because the limit has to approach something (4, 6, 10%) and can
never exceed it.

> OTOH, if you're
> trying to make a Swiss army knife deck, things get a lot more interesting.
> You get to try Rush with Intercept, or Voting with Bleeding, or Bounce
> and Bruise, or whatever. You get lots of different choices, even in
> mono-Clan decks. I find deck construction lots more challenging under CL
> than under NL.

All of those decks are decks that occur frequently in a NL environment.
This is not something unique to CL (that is, to find mixed strategy).
Rush with Intercept would be a hard challenge in any environment (IMHO
Good intercept, as opposed to light intercept, is often not helped by
attempting to be a viable rush deck too). I have two Rush/Vote decks,
One Vote/Bleed, etc... etc...

Your basic arguement (hinted at in this thread, seen in others) about a
viable CL deck not being viable in NL hinges on the fact that you can
make the above decks in CL and you wouldn't see them in NL because those
decks would be eaten up by the "focused" decks. I don't see this at
all. In NL, decks that try to mix strategies in a manner that
compliments that opposing strategy tend to be more robust. Decks in NL
that have no "focus" per se (that is, they aren't what you call a
conventional bleed/combat/vote/whatever deck), but have some kind of
honed plan can be made and be viable. As you said, making a Swiss army
knife deck can make things more interesting. In NL, it can be done, be
viable in its environment, and is a very challenging exercise.
