In article <4e53qv$m...@newsbf02.news.aol.com>, ncas...@aol.com
(NCascone) wrote:

> Deck construction options: to me, a matter of taste. Do you like to be
> able to construct OTP's? Do you like decks that have a tighter focus?
> These are questions that have no right answer.

I don't like to construct OTPs, _but_ I _do_ feel that if I really wanted
to make them, I should be able to. I feel that there is nothing wrong
with the OTP. They may be strong in their trick, but it is usually easy
for any number of diverse decks to derail the OTP from its course.

I like decks with a focus, whether it is tight or broad. I also like
decks with no real "focus", but an idea that is kind of fun (The "Kitchen
Sink" deck comes to mind, or my own "CDC" deck based on Vampiric Disease
and Atlanta). Unfortunately, tight CL cause these decks to be
unmakable. Broad CL (10%) tend to be so close to NL that I wonder why
they are clung to (especially w/o the Golden Tenets (read: Broken Game)).

> New players: most feel more comfortable with CL, despite the convincing
> arguments of NL players. I'm not sure what I think about this, except
> that it's a lot more fun to introduce new players with less-focused decks,
> since the games (again, to me) are more varied and interesting.

I somewhat disagree. I have taught a large number of people (a whole new
batch recently). Of them all, only one player wasn't convinced of NL. I
think that the "comfort" that you are familiar with in new players comes
from their drawing upon previous CCG experience. As for the kind of
decks that I teach people on, I tend to like to teach simple (NOTE: Not
the AWFUL basic game in V:tES) concepts one at a time (I think Jyhad is a
game that this is easy in). To accomplish this means, I have them play
the _tightest_ focus decks I have... at first, to get them familiar with
the concept of combinations and their importance. After playing two or
three different tight decks, I have them play a broader deck, to show
them that one need not have such a narrow focus, and that one can be
equally viable with broad goals. Finally, I help them create a deck from
my stock (given time), based on what they like. In a more time-short
environment, I try to give them one or two simple decks - one tight, the
other broad, to give the impression of the above. In all cases, the
games are varied and interesting (though somewhat less than if the
players were more experienced, and playing them same decks).

> Golden Tenets: multi-actions are not a problem under CL, IME. Still
> working on weenie votes, hope to get that deck via e-mail soon and try it
> out myself.

Tell us the results... :) Hope you enjoy my deck.

> "Lighting bolt effect": I'm sorry, I don't know what you mean. Do you
> mean the effect of having 4 copies each of cards that have similar
> effects? Again, this really only hurts low $ players if there is: a
> common or uncommon card such that it's effects are matched only by other
> cards that are rare. Got an example?

This is not a $ arguement. This is an arguement about the effect of more
cards destroying the CL environment. I.e., if 4CL works but 8CL doesn't,
what happens as more cards are made that duplicate the effects of other
"fragile" cards. When a third similar card comes out, now a defacto 12CL
becomes created. This has been termed the Lightning Bolt effect because
of Magic, with its Lightning Bolt, Chain Lightning, Incinerate, Ball
Lightning cards. They are (nearly) all different styles of card
(summoning, instant, sorcery), but their basic effect is similar. As
more KRCs and Freak Drives and whatevers come out, CL will lose their
viability. Especially given WotC's wonderful playtesting ability.

> Carlotta: same effect whether in NL or CL, maybe more effective in CL, but
> not a real big issue IMO.

In NL, Carlotata is effective, but in CL she is extraordinary. She can
certainly be intercepted, rushed, etc., but in a CL environment, being
able to have access to a theoretically infinite amount of cards is far
better than having absolute access to 4. In NL, this is far offset by
the fact that, up to deck size, you can have as many of whatever you want
in your deck.

> NL under the Golden Tenets may not be degenerate, but with the existence
> of OTP's, it's (value alert!) less interesting.

I feel that I play some decent decks, and that most of the people that I
play with do as well. I would like to see some NL OTPs to see what would
happen in my environment. I (currently) don't expect that much. Anyone,
please e-mail me or post ... Thanks.

> That's why I think my compromise (reprinted below) is a good basis for a
> more balanced play environment. I'm hoping it filters out dull OTPs
> without restricting *interesting* decks unreasonably.

The compromise (snipped below) of playing CL with NL on some cards is
really no different than playing with a large restricted list in a NL
environment. IMHO, this solution is merely half-a-step from NL. If you
prefer playing CL, fine. If you prefer playing with NL, fine. But, if
you would prefer the compromise solution, you need to ask yourself, "Why
am I not taking that half step?" If it is because you feel NL rewards
dull decks, fix that problem and play pure NL. If it is because you
think CL reward certain deck types, fix that problem and play CL. This
system (the compromise) does hold some merit, but for myself, I find that
the compromise is not necessary, and play NL. For those on the other
side of the fence, they will likely feel that the decision to play some
cards NL is relatively arbitrary and difficult to keep track of (who,
after all, decides which cards are NL. Who keeps track of which are
played that way).

[CL vs NL discussion of game environment vs game]

> : Yes, one can make effective and _dull_ NL decks. But this is a

personal
> : choice. One can make decks that are just as effective but not dull.
NL
> : does not mean OTP.
>

> Unfortunately, around here it does. :)

Sorry. :( Around here, there are dull, effective decks. But, I have not
seen any of these dull decks be any more effective than fun decks. The
difference is that the dull decks are... dull. That's it. _Far_ more
decks are interesting rather than dull, and they become more so as the
players gain more experience. Maybe the NL decks in your area are OTP
because NL deck construction faces more difficult choices. Under these
choices, it is often far easier to make a deck that does only one thing,
and does it well, than to make a robust deck.

> This just underscores what I meant about one solution being to find a good
> play group. But with Vampire/Jyhad making a comeback, I don't have a means
> to litmus test every potential opponent, so it can be good to have some
> kind of common ground to erect a workable game environment from. When
> among good friends, I feel free to play NL. At my store, I hear calls for
> CL...

As a NLer, I'm sorry to hear that (though I can see some CLers smiling
:). Usually, when I try to convert people that play CL, I tell them
about the Golden Tenets (something I feel is necessary whether you play
CL or NL). To back up this statement I show them a degenerate deck in
the tightest common CL environment I have seen, 4CL. This is typically
the "Weenie Vote Push". Repeat actions _are_ more of a problem in NL,
but I feel they are still a lesser evil in CL (especially as you approach
10%). I then argue how non-degenerate untap can be done with the GT. My
typical final arguements are how it is impossible to make a degenerate
deck in NL(I have _never_ seen one with the Golden Tenets, and it has
been a long standing challenge that no one has ever answered). Why play
CL? I have converted and not converted many to my line of thinking.

(Please don't think I do this with everyone I meet who plays CL. If I
were to go to your game store and be told that you play CL, I would
likely respond, "Well, I only have NL decks, can I play with it anyway?"
After playing (whether I play my NL deck or not), if anyone brings the
subject up, I'll debate with them, but I try not to push my opinions down
anyone's throat. Except here. ;)

> : > I've considered my own feelings on this subject for weeks now, and the
> : > only compromise (and I have to admit, I feel one is necessary) is:
> : > well, either play with no limits and avoid "boring" players (a
problem in
> : > that often one finds this out too late), or play with some loose limits
> : > (6CL, 10% whatever) but allow one or two cards to "break the
rule"... just
> : > name your transgressing card (usually Rush), and away you go! It's
an idea
> : > anyway, mainly to promote within-game variety.
> :
> : A good compromise... Me, I'm a stodgy, old purist ... :)
>
> I certainly understand this, but even your purist self plays with card
> errata, yes?

Only misprints and what we feel cards (like Rotschreck) should mean.
Other than that, the Golden Tenets are good enough for me, though I think
certain cards (see my opinions on LSJ's house rules list) ought to be redone.

>>>and therefore doesn't benefit from the add'l strikes the cel in the frisbee
>>>deck is granting.
>>
>> You can use the other cards at the same time; it's like a constant

>The question is whether you want to use up a slot in a deck with a permanent
>that must be equiped and only does 1R each round, or a strike card that your

Actually, no matter what environment you are in, Murder of Crows is
better than "a strike card that you opponent doesn't know is coming" that
does 1R (and IMHO it's better than 2R also, but that's just my opinion),
because the Murder of Crows damage can't be dodged. Not a particularly
good example of "4cl being more permanent-based than ncl". Yes, you have
to equip them, but if you're playing Gangrel, who's going to block the
equip? And if you're in a game witha speedy predator (like Malks),
you'll probably have trouble getting into combat anyway, so the strike
card (whether it's MOC or a 1R strike) will probably just end up
discarded anyway. A minor point in this discussion, which basically
centers around: "A deck that is based on one or two cards is hurt under

Ahem. Fun? I wonder, just a bit, if you have played a frisbee deck
(around here, the "fun in the sun" deck)? A 2 damage gate with a
manoeuvre is kinda fun, but a 3 damage sewer lid with a press is big fun,
especially in threes. A pissweak 1 damage canine horde or 1 damage bat
just isn't the same (or a fraction as effective, needless to say).

Our definitions of fun vary wildly, methinks.

Torn off signposts are fun. (1 damage hand strikes are not fun).
Blurs are fun. (1 strike a round is not fun).

All IMHO, natch.

: > A deck built around a not-entirely gameplay based theme that

: >is still viable adds to the variety of decks in the play enviroment, many
: >of which cannot work under 4cl (yes, back to this again).

: Would these cards make a 4cl ranged strike card deck possible? Was
: that not the goal here?

I didn't think so. I thought the goal was to show you poor deluded 4CL
folks that your 4CL is weak and pathetic, because you can't do a good
deck based on Thrown Gate, Thrown Sewer Lid and Well Aimed Car in 4CL.

(Ob smiley: :-) If that was necessary, shame on you for having no sense
of humour).

(Waits for laughter to die down). Seriously, folks, if you have not
played a Brujah pitch deck, you haven't had fun yet. Get 14 or 15 sewer
lids and gates (each, total c.30), about 15 additional strike cards, 7 or
8 Flashes, 8 or 10 Bum's Rushes, and a few Psyches to wriggle around
S:CE. Add the odd Pot/Cel master card, and Tastes of Vitae, and go to
town. The 4CL folks will have a heart attack, and call it a One Trick
Pony, but you can tell them to get a dog up 'em. Almost all commons, by
the way, and the rares aren't strictly necessary.

(I was considering saying something like, "No 4CL deck is this much fun",
but it'd turn into yet another endless 4CL argument, and I'm sick of the
topic).

: :-) -TJH

Yours, Kevin Lowe, (Brisbane, Australia).

>> I'm not sure what you mean by opponent matching. If you're trying to
make

I understand frequency tuning; you still get to do it under CL. Plus,
under CL there is some impetus to make the smallest deck that you think
won't run out (since the really big decks lower your chances of getting
the precise cards you want). NL has no such downward pressure on deck
size, since you can always work by percentage, no matter how large your
deck. BTW, I asked what you meant by "opponent matching", I'm really
interested to find out.

>Your basic arguement (hinted at in this thread, seen in others) about a
>viable CL deck not being viable in NL hinges on the fact that you can
>make the above decks in CL and you wouldn't see them in NL because those
>decks would be eaten up by the "focused" decks. I don't see this at
>all. In NL, decks that try to mix strategies in a manner that

>compliments that opposing strategy tend to be more robust. (snip to end)

But they're still beaten by OTP's whose key card or deck-style isn't
present. As you might have guessed, I've played under NL and been hosed
by irritating OTP decks. I'd just as soon not repeat the experience; CL's
are a clear, simple way to ensure it.

Let's face it, in any given group if CCGers, one or more is going to be a
hosehead who thinks it's really fun, neat, and cool to make the VtES
equivalent of a Lighting Bolt deck. I'd rather nip their doofy plans in
the bud by playing under a CL.

I submit this; your robust NL deck can still be beaten by the most
unimaginative OTP that you can't counter. That is _no_fun_, any way you
slice it; plus, it doesn't reward your hard work in putting together an
interesting, well-balanced NL deck. Where _do_ you play, anyway?

All your decks do indeed attack resources for a weenie vote deck. Several
attack its vampire resource and several its ability to pass votes.
However none attack the resource most critical to a 4cl weenie voter - the
supply of aggressive votes in its deck. There's only 4 KRC, 4 CA, 4
Sabbat Threats, 4 Parity Shift and (maybe) 4 Domain Challenge. If you can
intercept a fair number of those the weenie voter won't get anywhere,
regardless of the # of vampires or princes it's got.

With 4cl decks with lots of intercept and little combat are quite viable
(extremely good, actually). Normally they'd frequently get their faces
beaten in. With 4cl, however card-based combat doesn't work- (almost)
everybody need permanents to fight. Anybody without a gun can be
intercepted with impunity (Gangrel is the only exception). This is a very
good strategy because the copious intercept allows you to deny your
neighbors the permanents they need to fight effectively.

This is precisely the situation that evolved in my group with 4cl - the
majority of decks were Malks or Tremere, packing 1/4 or so intercept
cards. Such decks can easily intercept enough aggressive votes to make
any 4cl vote deck helpless.

>Prey: A permanent intercept deck (only needing +1, really) with lots of
>untap ability in the form of cat's guidance, homonculous, Freak Drive,
>The Beast Lord, etc. I felt that its untap would keep it going.

Too permanent dependent for a speed deck like weenie rush. By the time
you've gotten a homonculous and a Raven the weenie voter will have its
prey on the ropes. It should certainly get a few weenies, but by then
it's too late.

>Grand Prey: A temporary intercept and haven uncovered Cel/Tha deck. It
>doesn't go big on intercept because it only wants to block at +1/+2.
>When a S&B comes around it deflects/ Havens them. In this game, I felt
>the direct combat and light intercept would help.

Again, a deck attacking the ready vampire resource. A reasonable attack,
but
not the resource a 4cl vote deck is short of.

>Great Grand Prey: A Rush & Politics deck. The rush should kill the
>weenies. The Politics should make the pushing harder.

Rush combat is generally short on enter combat resources. You need a lot
of Rush to handle any kind of weenie. A "mad rush" deck with over 15 rush
cards could probably handle it but such decks aren't robust in general
play (and not even legal, 4-card). Worse, weenie decks can generally
afford to retrieve torporized vampires.

>Predator: A Presence Vote Deck. It easily gets the votes out. It still
>didn't have enough.

To be expected.

(NCascone) wrote:

> In article <Pine.NXT.3.91.960126160033.695D-100000@pentandria>, The
> Corrupter <sull...@cslab.uwlax.edu> writes:

[Response to deck construction under tight CL creating more intercept/perms]

> >But it also limits _choice_. It is a different, and in the terms you
> >presented, it is a difference of tast, but outside of your statements, it
> >means a limit to what a person can choose to create.

> Obviously. I don't want to go around this mulberry bush again. CL's
> prevent OTP's, the most objectionable form of deck (IME), and the most
> prevalent under NL (again, IME).

As you said in another thread, if a OTP deck isn't winning all the time,
who cares? One, OTPs are not a threat in a NL environment, if one uses
the Golden Tenets (or some other means of stopping abuse of vote pushes
current ruling and offensive untap). Two, OTPs exist in CL (see 4CL
Malk, 4CL Rush attempt).

[>>Frequency tuning]

> I understand frequency tuning; you still get to do it under CL.

Of course, but you have more control. To be explicit, in a S&B deck, you
can choose to discard your depth of cards (i.e., equivalent numbers of
varied stealth action modifiers) in return for a specific effect (9
faceless night and 3 of each other). The end result: less likelihood for
higher stealth, more likelihood of the "tapping" effect.

> Plus,
> under CL there is some impetus to make the smallest deck that you think
> won't run out (since the really big decks lower your chances of getting
> the precise cards you want).

Deck size is really not to important an arguement here, as long as one
observes typical max/min deck size. In a CL environment, decks tend to
be more permanent based. Every permanent deck I have seen tends to be
smaller. This, while an interesting note, isn't really a factor in the
CL/NL debate.

> NL has no such downward pressure on deck
> size, since you can always work by percentage, no matter how large your
> deck. BTW, I asked what you meant by "opponent matching", I'm really
> interested to find out.

I think this statement somehow got misattributed to me, but to me
opponent matching means making a deck that is robust enough to handle a
large number of situations. This is really vague, and I don't think it
means what the person who said it (?) originally meant, but... :/

> >Your basic arguement (hinted at in this thread, seen in others) about
a
> >viable CL deck not being viable in NL hinges on the fact that you can
> >make the above decks in CL and you wouldn't see them in NL because
those
> >decks would be eaten up by the "focused" decks. I don't see this at
> >all. In NL, decks that try to mix strategies in a manner that
> >compliments that opposing strategy tend to be more robust. (snip to end)

> But they're still beaten by OTP's whose key card or deck-style isn't
> present. As you might have guessed, I've played under NL and been hosed
> by irritating OTP decks. I'd just as soon not repeat the experience; CL's
> are a clear, simple way to ensure it.

I've never seen this. I have played since the _day_ Jyhad was released,
and while some decks I have might not ever be able to handle a specific
deck (explicit example: I have a Fortitude based combat deck that
_never_ stands a chance against a Tremere Combat deck. I am working to
correct this...), I have yet to see a OTP or other "degenerate" deck ever
be something that needs a specific key card to be beaten. Rather, a set
of key cards tend to blow them out of the water. Please, post or mail a
deck or deck idea so I can see how I feel my decks would handle it.

> Let's face it, in any given group if CCGers, one or more is going to be a
> hosehead who thinks it's really fun, neat, and cool to make the VtES
> equivalent of a Lighting Bolt deck. I'd rather nip their doofy plans in
> the bud by playing under a CL.

Of course. But, as I've said before, I have _never_ seen a deck that is
penultimate under NL/GT.

> I submit this; your robust NL deck can still be beaten by the most
> unimaginative OTP that you can't counter. That is _no_fun_, any way you
> slice it; plus, it doesn't reward your hard work in putting together an
> interesting, well-balanced NL deck. Where _do_ you play, anyway?

I play in a large number of different playing groups. I started a Jyhad
League in my area, introduced the game to friends, play it in a weekly
CCG group (which oftentimes has more than 100 people attending) in which
new people may appear out of the blue, I play with a core group of
fanatics, and when I go home on breaks I play with a number of people who
have played since the game began. I have played 10%CL, 6CL, and NL. I
have played with weenies and people who pull apart decks when they feel
the deck is good enough. I repeat again, I have _never_ seen a
"degenerate" deck in NL/GT.

Would CLs that eliminate the viability of "degenerate" decks and make
OTPs not an issue be a good solution? I.e., an environment where no deck
can be made that is penultimate? I suggest an infinite-CL, with Golden
Tenets and your own house rules list (no different than a list from the
DTR, really). It's worked for me for over a year.

> This means that the CL would have to be
> loose enough to create an enemy for the MS&B (TTBOMK, the current reigning
> stable strategy that isn't the subject of a GT (yet)), but tight enough to

from forming or degenerate strategies from forming (I think you mean the
latter, but would like clarification)?

> enough to have a good chance of winning on its own; therefore, there were

> size of a CL. Time for a new thread?

Well, actually, I have to say I've been moving toward 6CL, especially
after seeing James' famed MS&B-killing Brujah Rush deck (had exactly 1
card at frequency 7, otherwise 6CL-legal). I think the inevitability was
in James' mind, and the reduction to absurdity was more to make a
rhetorical point than anything else.

We haven't even addressed what CL is "best", mostly we've been discussing
_any_ CL vs. NL. In my mind, the "best" CL would allow a wide range of
deck choices, but eliminate (to the extent possible) OTP's and degenerate

decks (aka "stable strategies"). This means that the CL would have to be

loose enough to create an enemy for the MS&B (TTBOMK, the current reigning
stable strategy that isn't the subject of a GT (yet)), but tight enough to
keep other stable strategies from forming.

can make under 4CL). Please not my parenthetical phrase "to the extent
possible". Eliminating the vast bulk of OTP's is worth the CL to me.

>Would CLs that eliminate the viability of "degenerate" decks and make
>OTPs not an issue be a good solution? I.e., an environment where no deck

>can be made that is penultimate? I suggest an infinite-CL, with Golden
>Tenets and your own house rules list (no different than a list from the
>DTR, really). It's worked for me for over a year.

In what was way does 2GT "make OTP's not an issue"? To me, the truth is
quite the opposite.

>> This means that the CL would have to be
>> loose enough to create an enemy for the MS&B (TTBOMK, the current
reigning
>> stable strategy that isn't the subject of a GT (yet)), but tight enough
to
>> keep other stable strategies from forming.
>

>What does the last phrase mean? Do you want to stop stable strategies
>from forming or degenerate strategies from forming (I think you mean the
>latter, but would like clarification)?

I mean both. Obviously, no one likes the possibility of degenerate decks;
that's what the 2GT is all about. Additionally, since a stable strategy
(degenerate or not) will tend to ruin the game (by forcing decks to either
copy it or deal with it), they are also to be avoided. I think that's why
the new cards in VtES deal so harshly with heightened bleed; plus-Bleed
decks were becoming stable strategies.

In 4cl, MS&B and WV may be extremely good decks, but in NL/GT, who really
cares if one makes these decks. They are not more likely to win than any
other. If OTPs are effectively made into a deck no more powerful than
any other, why try to eliminate them? Boredom when playing one? Well,
yes, a OTP will be boring to play and play against. But as a OTP is not
any better than any other deck, one eventually (usually quickly) matures
into playing decks that are not only more fun (i.e., not a OTP), but just
as reliable.

> that's what the 2GT is all about. Additionally, since a stable strategy
> (degenerate or not) will tend to ruin the game (by forcing decks to either
> copy it or deal with it), they are also to be avoided. I think that's why
> the new cards in VtES deal so harshly with heightened bleed; plus-Bleed
> decks were becoming stable strategies.

What is wrong with a new stable strategy. As more cards come, the game
will continue to evolve, and if new stable strategies don't come into
existence, I will be disappointed. These strategies must be carefully
constructed so as not to upset the balance of what can and cannot be
played, but they also need to not be pushovers. Given that R. Garfield
has less of a hand in this game than he once did (and given WotC's record
on this game), I am leery of what might happen if they do try to
introduce another major strategy, but I would love it if they pull it off.

If you mean stable as "unshakable", I agree. No strategy should be
unshakable. I mean stable as being consistent and reliable. In this
manner, I feel that stability is a huge necessity.

As for the new V:tES anti-bleed cards, I think they were poorly
conceived, and ill-written (with the exception of Elder Intervention),
but that is another story...

You don't understand what I mean by a stable strategy. I don't mean a

I would call your "stable" strategy a degeneracy that slipped by game
designers. I have never seen such a strategy in NL/GT. In my mind, the
three major strategies are ones that need to be answered. You cannot
play a very good deck if you don't have them in mind. The best example
to this is the hostile vote deck at a table where no one is prepared for
politics. Vote after vote will pass unblocked, leaving the hostile vote
deck to defend against combat (most likely with majesty/elysium). I have
seen the same thing happen at a table when no one was playing strong
bleed defense (bleeding decks had died in frequency at that time, and
most were playing politics or combat). Similarly with combat.

I think (perhaps incorrectly?) that you don't want to see any new
strategies that a deck must have some answer to to be built. I don't see
this as a problem. A new player from outside the area had built an
impressive blood gain and vampire recruit deck. It had minimal
obfuscate, auspex, celerity, and dominate. It played with most of the
clans. It had never lost. Typically it had so much blood that it
couldn't be stopped. After playing it for the first time, many of the
people altered their decks. More blood gain was put in their decks
(frankly because his numerous methods of blood gain had never been tried
successfully), several people made more location hosing decks (robust
against most decks), and the environment changed. After that first game,
he wins as frequently with that deck as anyone else's deck does.

The point? His aggressive blood gain strategy altered the environment we
played in. It was a new strategy for us, as we had never seen blood gain
accomplished in that manner. As a result, many people altered their
decks. Others didn't. Even when he plays that deck with decks who
haven't changed, just knowing what is going to happen is enough for the
prey or predator to deal with him. His OTP is not a win-machine. It won
that first game because it surprised us, and we didn't have a proper
strategy in mind with the decks we had at the table. With the same
decks, and without altering the prey/predator relationship, it would be a
very different game. His win was from surprise, not OTPness.

I started rambling towards the end (all apologies), but my basic
statements in regards to OTPs are this: Make them in NL/GT. They are
not win-machines. I have never seen a win-machine in this environment,
and challenge anyone to make one.

Messages.Author: The Corrupter
Messages.Body:
On Mon, 4 Mar 1996, Super Ted wrote:

> We play with a 4cl with a 1 unique and 1 vampire limit as well. There are
> good - if somewhat contentious - reasons for this approach in our view.

I have seen this idea (that of a one-card limit for uniques) quite often
among card limits camps. As an opponent of card limits in general, I am
surprised at how often this 1CL is used by numerous CL camps. What is
the purpose of a Unique 1CL?

It changes the flavor of the game, yes. But does it make it better (in a
CL environment)? I can't see how it would be beneficial. Richard
Garfield's rules on contesting were a stroke of genius (as others have
said), and the self-limiting nature of unique cards seems to overweigh a
need for a _further_ limit.

Arguements could be made for a game-realism model, but where do they
lead? The cards on the table are the cards that are having to deal with
a state of existance. Having more than one Carlotta, for example, in your
crypt is not the same as having more than one Carlotta out on the table.
For them both to be out on the table (say, without contesting), is to say
that there are two "twins" with exactly the same name, powers, etc..
This would not be realistic. Having more than one Carlotta in your crypt
(or uncontrolled region) is saying that you, as a Methuselah, are
investing that much more energy and resources to Carlotta. You are that
much more interested in controlling her. It does not mean that you will
somehow get more than one up.

As for game considerations, having multiples of the same unique card allow
you to make more plans is your deck. A Unique 1CL tends to make Jyhad far
more based on luck than on planning.

Any responses from Unique 1CL proponents is appreciated. Of course,
everyone can play how they want, and you may enjoy it better that way,
but how is it better? Any opponents to Unique 1CL from the CL crowd?
Thanks.

Hello,

The idea behind playing a one card unique limit is that there is only one of
these places (using as an example a unique location) in the world.

Therefore we take the view that as there is only one place, only one card to
represent the location should be placed in each deck. I can obviously see
the slight discrepancy here: each Methuselah might place one in his/her
deck. This then is where the contesting aspect of the game comes into play.

The same logic applies to the vampires. Each vampire is unique so why have
more than one in each deck?

That then is the crux of our argument. I can understand why people dislike
it but as a house rule we find that it works well.

But....

In the game world of Jyhad, when you put more than 1 of a unique card
in your deck, that doesn't mean that you actually own 2, in fact, having 1 of
a unique card in your deck doesn't mean that you own it. Having a unique card
in your deckmeans that you, as a Methuselah, have tabs on it, and may be able
to wrangle your self into control of it. Having 2 or more means that you have
more information on taking it over, and are more likely to do so. The weaknes
of this, both in game terms and out, is that you are potentially going to get
a hand glut - or rather, invest so much time in the conquering of the Barrens
that you are short on other sinister plans.

If, however, you get really bothered by someone up and starting a fire
in the Art Museum, and then some other Methuselah (or GASP, the same one) slap
down the Art Museum - just remember that the Art Museum is a place, if smashed
it can be rebuilt, and who's to say that some enterprising vampire didn't save
the paintings while the sinister kindred responsible for the flames fanned the
flames of the now empty shell of the art museum?

Basically, each card in your deck does not represent an actual thing
it represents the mad plottings of a Methuselah. In short, cards aren't real
until they are made real, by putting them in play. Until they join the ranks
of what really is, they are just things that could be. And will you say that
some things that "might happen" can't be twice as likely as other stuff from
similar straights?

Messages.Author: Jarrod P. Stenberg
Messages.Body:
My thoughts on Unique card limits...

Arguments that a unique card represents the only existing version of
the item, and therefore should have a CL of one per deck is kind of odd.
My reasoning is that a card (unique or otherwise) represents a resource or
tool for the Methuselah. If Bob the Methuselah stacks his deck with four
Powerbase:Chicago, it doesn't mean that he literally has four cities of
Chicago in his deck, but that he has invested more of his resources to
insure access to Chicago. If he deals himself a hand with all four of the
unique card, maybe he should learn to diversify his resources a bit. If
he brings a unique card in play and it gets burned and he brings a
duplicate out, he found a new way to gain access to it. It's a bloody
game. Worry less about literal interpretations of the cards on reality.
